title: The Radio That Knew Tomorrow (Long)
sources: Original fiction (SCIFI, 'the science is real'). All characters, towns and the radio station are invented.

Wikipedia, 'Time in Kiribati' (Line Islands, UTC+14:00, the most advanced time zone in the world); timeanddate.com 'International Date Line' (Baker Island at UTC-12, Tokelau and Samoa on the west side; 25 hours when crossing)
Wikipedia, 'Time in Samoa' (Samoa skipped Friday 30 December 2011, going from Thursday 29 December to Saturday 31 December, to align with Australia and New Zealand)
Wikipedia, 'Skywave' (shortwave signals are bent back by the ionosphere and skip across oceans; best below about 10 MHz at night)
General knowledge: a tsunami crosses a deep ocean about as fast as a jet airliner (NOAA; page not retrievable in this run), radio travels at light speed.

lines.text: The old radio said it was Tuesday.
It was Monday.
By the end of that week, a whole town stood on a hill, in their pyjamas,
and every one of them was there because of that radio.
But to understand how, we need to go back a few days.
Meet Mari Vega. Fourteen years old, and the best radio fixer in Port Lantern.
Her grandpa Tito owned the shop, a tiny place stuffed with dusty wires.
He had exactly one rule: never buy a radio that smells like fish.
So on Saturday, Mari bought a radio that smelled like fish.
It was huge, and wooden, and ugly, with one cracked dial.
The old sailor at the flea market sold it for three coins,
and left before she could change her mind.
She dragged it home, scrubbed it clean, and plugged it in.
Nothing. Just static. Like bacon frying.
She tried every knob. Still nothing.
Until Monday evening, at seven o'clock, one last turn of the dial,
and a cheerful voice said, Good evening! It's Tuesday!
Mari checked the calendar. Monday.
She checked her phone. Monday.
She checked her grandpa. He said Monday, and had she eaten?
So either the radio was broken, or it knew something she didn't.
The voice kept chatting. A big storm just crossed our island, heading east. Rain by breakfast.
Mari rolled her eyes, and went to bed.
At breakfast, it rained.
Okay. Lucky guess. But that wasn't the strange part.
That night, the radio read out a football score.
The Reef Sharks beat the Palm Crabs, three to one.
The newspaper didn't print it until the next morning.
Her friend Dev bet his lunch money on the Sharks, and ate like a king.
Then the radio named the winner of the Great Pie Contest. Lemon meringue, by Mrs. Okoye.
By Thursday, Dev had told the school, and the school had told the town.
A line stretched outside the shop. Forty people. Then a hundred.
One man brought a goat, for some reason.
Everyone wanted tomorrow's news, and everyone wanted it first.
Mayor Pruitt offered a thousand coins for the radio.
Mari said no. Her grandpa said nothing. He just frowned at the dial.
Radios don't know tomorrow, mija, he muttered. So what is it listening to?
That night, the radio went quiet. Then the voice came back, shaking.
Emergency! A giant wave is racing across the ocean!
It smashed our docks this morning, and it's heading east. Every coast, get to high ground!
Mari froze. Port Lantern was east.
And that radio had never been wrong. Not once.
She had about three hours.
She ran into the street and shouted, everybody up the hill!
And for once, everybody listened, mostly because of the pie.
Grandma carried her cat. Dev carried a toaster. The goat carried nothing, but it led the way.
They climbed in the dark, hundreds of people in pyjamas.
Then they waited. And waited.
At ten o'clock, the sea went strangely quiet.
Then the harbour rose, and rose, and swallowed the docks,
and spilled into the streets, and lifted the boats like toys.
But every single person was safe, up on that hill.
A radio had saved a whole town. But how?
The next morning, Mari and Tito unrolled his old map of the world.
There's a line, he said, drawn through the middle of the ocean. The date line.
Cross it going west, and you skip straight into tomorrow.
Inside the radio, Mari found a faded sticker. Radio Sunrise, on a tiny island, just past that line.
And that island? It sits twenty-two hours ahead of Port Lantern.
See, the radio never saw tomorrow.
It only heard a place where tomorrow had already started.
At night, radio waves bounce off the sky like skipping stones, all the way across the ocean.
Their news raced here at the speed of light. The wave was only as fast as a jet.
Which gave Port Lantern just enough time to run.
And the date line gets weirder. In twenty eleven, the country of Samoa jumped across it,
and skipped Friday the thirtieth of December. On purpose. That part is real.
Mari mailed the island a thank you letter, with a very big drawing of a wave.
A month later, a reply arrived.
Dear Mari, thank you! We read your letter on Tuesday, and it confused everyone.
Because according to our calendar, you're from yesterday.
So the old radio said it was Tuesday, and Mari said it was Monday.
And the funny thing? They were both right.
If you liked this, the Hollow Archive has a new story every day.
